title: Remote-epitaxy peel-and-stack single-crystal oxide channel films
idea: IFR: 'every tier has a single-crystal channel and the substrate lasts forever.' Backward: grow single-crystal beta-Ga2O3 or In2O3 channel films by remote epitaxy through a graphene layer on a reusable seed crystal, exfoliate each film, and transfer it as the channel of each 3D tier.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): single-crystal ultra-wide-gap channels remove the grain-boundary leakage tail of deposited oxides; seed reuse removes substrate cost.

title: Eliminate the high-AR capacitor etch: anodic alumina pore templates
idea: Skip plasma-etching capacitor holes; deposit thick aluminium over the transistor array, pre-dent it at each storage node, and anodize so self-ordered pores with aspect ratios above 500:1 grow straight down onto each node; line them with high-k and electrode.
why: Capacitor charge wall: the AR 115:1 needed for more charge comes from electrochemistry instead of a hard mask and etch, giving a ~2x Cs headroom with no hard mask.

title: Flip the wafer: etch storage capacitors from the backside
idea: Build access transistors and bitlines on the front, bond to a carrier, thin the silicon to ~2-3 um, then etch capacitor holes from the backside landing directly on each storage-node junction and fill with MIM. Capacitor height is set by backside film thickness instead of fighting front-side BEOL, and bitline contacts no longer weave between capacitor pillars.
why: Capacitor wall + 6F2 congestion (facts 1,4): removing storage-node contacts/landing pads from the front frees ~20-30% of cell area toward 4F2 and lets capacitor height grow independently of bitline routing.

title: Cast or reclaimed silicon replaces prime CZ wafers under BEOL arrays
idea: When the array is built in BEOL-temperature tiers and the periphery is bonded from another wafer, the array wafer's substrate is only a flat carrier: substitute prime CZ silicon with reclaimed wafers, cast multicrystalline silicon (lower-purity Si3N4-coated crucibles, not Spruce-Pine-grade liners) or glass carriers.
why: Quartz-crucible chokepoint (Spruce Pine >80%): roughly halves prime-wafer demand per bit for bonded array/periphery products and cuts substrate cost ~$50-100 per wafer.

title: Strain-release rolls planar arrays into vertical Swiss-roll micro-tubes
idea: Substitute deposited tiers with rolled turns: build a planar thin-film array (oxide-semiconductor 2T0C cells plus wiring) on a strained SiNx/SiNx bilayer over a sacrificial Ge layer; release makes the membrane self-roll into a 10-20-turn tube standing on edge contacts, so one planar litho flow yields 10-20 effective tiers per footprint.
why: 3D bit density without a 26+ tier deposition/etch stack (fact 2) or high-AR etch; capex per bit near a planar thin-film line; ~5-10x bits per footprint for capacity memory.

title: Strontium-calcium titanate superlattice gives k near 200 inside tiers
idea: Grow ALD SrTiO3/CaTiO3 nanolaminates with 1-2 nm periods whose interfacial strain stabilizes a high-k paraelectric state at ~8 nm thickness (k ~150-250) on TiN, crystallized by millisecond flash anneal; a lateral cylinder ~150 nm long inside a 40 nm tier then stores ~5 fF.
why: Meets the charge wall (fact 1) with a short lateral capacitor that fits one tier, making lateral 3D cells viable (fact 2) without Ru electrodes; Ca is abundant and Sr moderately available.

title: Drum read-retry lets tiny capacitors run at 1% sense errors
idea: Revive the drum and disk habit of re-reading on the next revolution: shrink Cs to ~2 fF so ~1% of reads are noise-limited errors, and on ECC failure re-sense the restored row with a longer bitline development time.
why: Fact 1: capacitor AR falls from ~70:1 toward ~30:1 with ~2.5x less charge; rare retries cost <2% bandwidth.

title: Mortise-and-tenon bond pads enable per-cell split-wafer DRAM
idea: Joinery self-aligns parts; etch conical tenons on a transistor wafer and matching mortises on a separate capacitor wafer so mechanical engagement during hybrid bonding pulls overlay from ~100 nm to ~10 nm, allowing one bond per cell at ~200 nm pitch, with transistors from logic-like lines and deep capacitors from MEMS-like lines.
why: Splits the cell's two incompatible processes (capacitor thermal budget vs transistor leakage, facts 1 and 3) onto optimized wafers; per-cell bonding is ~10x too coarse today, and self-alignment is the enabler.

title: Convert 3D NAND lines into 3D DRAM lines sharing tool sets
idea: [Box: plate-stack 3D DRAM | IGZO or poly-Si | CMOS-under-array | 3D-NAND-style stacking | Si | existing NAND high-AR etch, replacement-gate and staircase tools] Design the 3D DRAM flow around 3D NAND tool recipes and contract NAND makers' underused EUV-free lines, swinging capacity between NAND and DRAM as prices move.
why: Capital and time (fact 4): skips the 3-5 year, $15B+ greenfield fab; NAND lines already own the high-AR etch and deposition tools, and supply can flex quarterly.

title: Iron-catalyzed carbon nanotube bundles form vertical through-tier bitlines
idea: Evaporate ~1 nm Fe catalyst on Al2O3 at the bottom of vertical holes through a tier stack and grow dense multi-walled CNT bundles by thermal CVD at 550-650 C, filling each hole with an electromigration-immune vertical bitline or plate line contacted by every tier.
why: Replaces tungsten fill in deep holes (resource chokepoint) where CVD metal voids at high aspect ratio (fact 2); Fe and C are abundant and CNT CVD furnaces are common in university labs.

title: Negative-capacitance gate stack amplifies tiny gain-cell storage charge
idea: TRIZ #8 Anti-weight: counter the 'weight' of a tiny stored charge with an internal uplift: add a thin ferroelectric layer to the read transistor's gate, matched to operate in its negative-capacitance regime, so the storage node's voltage is amplified at the channel surface. The storage node can then be just the bare gate (~0.1 fF) with an unchanged read margin.
why: Fact 1 and 10: ~2-3x read current per stored electron, storage swing down to ~0.5 V (CV2 -75%) and smaller capacitorless cells.

title: Inside-out gain cell: storage core gates its surrounding channel tube
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: form each 4F2 pillar as an insulated metal core (the storage node) wrapped by gate oxide and a thin IGZO channel tube that is the read transistor. A small vertical write transistor stacked on top charges the core, so the core gates the whole tube circumference with no separate capacitor.
why: Fact 1 and 4: 2T0C in one 4F2 pillar (vs ~8-12F2 planar gain cells) with ~3x read current per stored charge from the gate-all-around tube.

title: Eliminate tungsten wordlines: in-situ doped SiGe wordline tiers
idea: In a Si/SiGe superlattice 3D DRAM, keep the wordline tiers as heavily boron-doped epitaxial SiGe grown in the same epi run, with no replacement-gate metal fill, and use short segmented wordlines with local drivers to tolerate the higher resistance.
why: Scarce resource (China ~80% of tungsten) and process steps: removes the W replacement-gate module and its voids in deep lateral cavities.

title: Post-it tier: tiny 1 ms-retention cells for transient data
idea: A Post-it is cheap because it need not last; dedicate a 3D tier to 0.5 fF cells with ~1 ms retention on short bitlines for data whose lifetime is shorter than that (activations, in-flight KV, gradients), placed there by the compiler and never refreshed.
why: Capacitor wall, refresh and access energy (facts 1, 3, 8): ~10x smaller Cs and shorter lines cut switched charge ~10x with zero refresh; claims ~10x lower energy per access for transient traffic.

title: NMOS-only sub-wordline drivers bootstrapped by cell capacitors
idea: Rearrange the sub-wordline driver: drop the PMOS and its N-well spacing and revive 1970s NMOS bootstrap drivers, using array-process cylinder capacitors as bootstrap capacitors so wordlines still reach ~3 V. Zero added masks: it is a layout change.
why: Periphery is ~49% of die (fact 7): sub-wordline driver stripes shrink ~30-40% (well spacing dominates them), giving roughly 3-5% more bits per die.

title: Recirculating vertical bucket-brigade string without cell capacitors
idea: Inverts 'every bit is randomly addressable in place.' A 64-128-gate vertical channel string stores charge packets in potential wells under its gates and clocks them tier-to-tier like a CCD to one sense/regenerate amplifier at the string foot, which rewrites each packet as it recirculates; random access is per string (~30-60 ns) and refresh comes free with circulation.
why: Facts 1-3: 3D with no capacitor and no lateral transistor; density scales with tier count; separate refresh energy folds into the shift itself.

title: Coextruded 500-layer polymer film forms stacked capacitor plates in one pass
idea: Use microlayer coextrusion (layer-multiplier dies proven on ~800-layer optical films) to make alternating conductive-polymer/dielectric-polymer laminates, imprint a trench grid that segments the stack into per-cell capacitors, and contact odd and even plates on opposite sidewalls after selective lateral recess.
why: Layer count is nearly free in coextrusion: C=N*eA/d with 500 layers of 50 nm, k=3 gives ~250 fF per um^2 footprint, so the tier count of fact 2 arrives in one extrusion pass rather than hundreds of deposition cycles.

title: Sushi conveyor: vertical charge-packet shift string replaces per-cell capacitors
idea: Forced connection to a sushi belt: in a NAND-like stack of 64 gate tiers around a low-leakage IGZO or poly-Si vertical channel, bits are stored as charge packets in gate-induced potential wells and clocked along the string CCD-style to one sense node at the base. There is no capacitor or access transistor per bit, only a gate electrode over a shared channel, and reads stream in order like plates passing a diner.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): bit cost tracks NAND-like tier cost (claim ~5-10x below 2D DRAM at 64+ tiers) with unlimited endurance; latency 20-70 ns by position, suited to streaming rows such as KV caches.

title: Continuous inline tier-deposition line: 200 tiers without breaking vacuum
idea: Shift tier fabrication from hours per batch tool to a continuous conveyor: like solar and display inline coaters, pass wafers through a linear chain of 200 sputter and ALD stations, so a whole tier superlattice is deposited in one transit with no queueing or handling between tiers.
why: Capital and cycle time of 3D stacking (fact 4): ~3-5x more deposition throughput per tool dollar.

title: Sixteen-cell local bitlines cut required storage charge tenfold
idea: Derive Cs from the charge-sharing equation dV=(V/2)*Cs/(Cs+Cbl) instead of accepting a 30-40 fF bitline: split each vertical bitline into 16-cell local segments (~0.3 fF, ~1 um tall) that each drive one local gain transistor onto the global bitline. The cell capacitor then only has to swing a sub-femtofarad node.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and 3D blocker (fact 2): Cs=0.5 fF still yields ~300 mV of signal versus ~5 fF today, so lateral or planar capacitors in 3D tiers become sufficient; ~10x less charge per cell also cuts restore energy.

title: Bitlines on the backside, wordlines on the front
idea: Rearrange the routing planes: after front-side transistor and capacitor formation, flip and thin the wafer and form bitlines on the backside contacting the bottom of each vertical channel, so bitlines and capacitors never compete for the same front-side layers.
why: Layout congestion and signal margin (facts 1,4): bitlines become wide low-R lines with air gaps (~30% less bitline capacitance = proportionally smaller Cs) and the front side can pack capacitors at 4F2.

title: Pantry kitchen: per-mat reduction engines in a bonded logic tier
idea: Cook where the food is stored: a logic tier bonded beneath each 3D DRAM mat carries one bit-serial adder/comparator per 64 sense amps, so dot-products, top-k and sums over a row finish in place and only the reduced result, 1/64 of the bits, leaves the mat.
why: Data movement and overfetch (facts 5, 8): bits moved per useful result drop ~64x; claims 10-30x lower energy per AI access such as attention scoring.

title: Spacer-split pillars give two cells per 4F2 footprint
idea: [Box: two half-capacitors | split VCT with two independent channel faces | charge-share SA | monolithic | Si | ArF pillars + self-aligned spacer slot] Pattern pillars at relaxed ArF pitch, then cut each in half with a self-aligned spacer-defined slot so its two faces become separate channels gated by left and right wordlines, each tied to its own half-capacitor.
why: No EUV (fact 4): 2F2 per bit at F=20 nm (~800 nm2/bit) matches 6F2 at F=12 nm (~864 nm2/bit) without EUV.

title: Well-less satellite tiers: oxide-isolated array layers remove STI for 4F2
idea: Satellites dodge single-event upsets by putting transistors on buried oxide with no bulk well; build every DRAM array tier on transferred thin silicon over oxide so there is no substrate junction, no well contact and no shallow-trench isolation between cells. Gate-all-around vertical channels abut at true 4F2 because isolation comes from the oxide below, and the bulk charge-collection volume behind soft errors and junction leakage disappears.
why: Layout density 6F2 to 4F2 (~33% more bits per tier), removes the junction/GIDL part of the retention tail (fact 3), and gives inherent soft-error immunity.

title: LC-resonant wordline planes recycle charge in 3D arrays
idea: TRIZ #18 Mechanical vibration (use resonance): 3D wordline planes are large, regular capacitors, so pair each plane group with an on-package RDL inductor and drive it as an LC tank with adiabatic sinusoidal ramps. Most of the ~3 V wordline charge flows back into the tank instead of being dumped to ground every activation.
why: Fact 10: sidesteps the CV2 floor by recovering ~60-80% of wordline energy; activation energy ~30-40% lower.

title: Pendulum wordline planes: resonant LC drive recycles plate charge
idea: Like a pendulum clock trading kinetic for potential energy, make the large horizontal wordline plates of a 3D array the capacitor of an LC tank with an interposer spiral inductor, swinging the selected plate sinusoidally to VPP and back so ~85% of its charge returns to the inductor instead of ground.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): ~3 V wordline CV2 dominates plate-wordline 3D DRAM; claims 5-10x lower wordline energy per activation.

title: Wavelength-addressed tiers: light pulses replace wordline voltage swings
idea: Inverts 'wordlines are electrical wires.' Give each tier photoconductive access devices whose band gap is tuned by alloy composition, and select a tier by the wavelength launched into an integrated vertical waveguide grid, so only the absorbing tier opens.
why: Facts 7 and 10: removes 3 V wordline CV² and per-tier decoders/staircase; speculative ~5-10x activation-energy gain.

title: Corrugated-board substrate: one array film over V-groove relief
idea: Like corrugated cardboard folding a flat sheet into a high-area core, KOH-etch Si(100) into 54.7-degree V-grooves at ~200 nm pitch and build a thin-film transistor-capacitor array conformally on both groove faces with tilted implants and spacer patterning, packing ~1.7x more planar-processed cells per footprint.
why: Density without tier stacking (fact 4): ~1.7x area from one cheap wet etch while reusing planar steps, sidestepping the 26-tier break-even.

title: Dedicated deep-trench capacitor wafer hybrid-bonded onto transistor wafer
idea: [Box: single-crystal Si trench charge | Si VCT | charge-share SA | wafer-on-wafer hybrid bond, one pad per storage node | low-grade Si capacitor wafer | Bosch DRIE + ALD] Etch capacitors as 100:1+ trenches into a separate Si wafer (single-crystal Si etches deeper and straighter than oxide molds, and the doped wafer itself is the plate), then bond it face-to-face to the access-transistor wafer using oversized self-aligned Cu pads per storage node.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) plus process decoupling: Cs >10 fF possible and the high-AR mold module leaves the transistor wafer, so each wafer runs on its own optimized line.

title: Kerfless-solar epitaxial lift-off: crucible-free crystalline tiers from reusable parents
idea: Kerfless solar startups grow epitaxial silicon on porous-silicon release layers and peel it, reusing the parent wafer many times; grow 1 um device-grade epi in H2-carrier trichlorosilane on a porous parent, bond it onto the finished DRAM stack, cleave at the porous layer to form the next tier, and re-porosify the parent for ~50 reuses. This replaces smart-cut, whose co-implants often use helium.
why: Spruce Pine quartz-crucible dependence cut ~50x per tier, crystalline bonded tiers for 3D DRAM (fact 2), helium-free.

title: Memory inside the glass-core package substrate beneath the processor
idea: IFR: 'memory takes zero extra package area and sits millimeters from compute.' Backward: deposit several oxide-semiconductor gain-cell tiers directly on the glass core of the package substrate (flat, 400 C tolerant), then build the redistribution layers on top, so the GPU's own substrate becomes a multi-GB memory plane reached through micro-bumps.
why: Data movement and HBM tax (facts 5, 6): removes HBM stacks and interposer; ~1 pJ/bit over <2 mm, with capacity that scales with package size.

title: Roll-formed corrugated tiers: long-channel lateral transistors in short pitch
idea: Roll-formed corrugated sheet gets length without footprint; deposit each tier over a pre-patterned sinusoidal base so the lateral access transistor's channel follows the wave, giving ~2x channel length (and extra flank width) inside the same cell pitch.
why: A longer effective channel suppresses short-channel leakage and the refresh-forcing tail (fact 3) by up to ~10x while keeping 3D cell pitch, making lateral transistors viable (fact 2).

title: Alien asks why the basement is empty: eDRAM inside the interposer
idea: An alien sees that the huge interposer under every AI package is passive silicon. A 10-person team designs an active mature-node interposer with deep-trench 1T1C cells, which interposers already carry as decoupling capacitors, and has a foundry build it.
why: ~2000 mm2 of otherwise wasted silicon holds ~1-2 GB of near-logic memory per package, at ~1 pJ/bit (Fact 5), with no EUV.

title: Engine remanufacturing: harvest and restack DRAM dies from e-waste
idea: Like remanufactured engines and toner cartridges: buy scrapped server DIMMs by the ton, debond and retest the dies, then edge-stack or hybrid-bond 8-16 known-good dies onto a new logic base die with fresh interface and strong ECC, sold as certified 'reman' capacity memory.
why: Harvested die cost approaches scrap value (~$0.05-0.2/GB), so restacked modules can be ~30-100x cheaper per GB than new 2026 contract DRAM; trade-offs: older densities, mixed speed bins, shorter warranty.

title: Battery jelly-roll winding: wind single-tier DRAM foil into cylinders
idea: Adapted from Li-ion jelly-roll cells: imprint a single-tier oxide-TFT array on a 5 um polyimide web at roll speed, then wind ~1,000 turns into a cylinder whose battery-style edge tabs bring segmented bitlines and wordlines out to a bonded controller.
why: Volume density comes from winding, not tier deposition; web processing at ~$5-10/m2 x 1,000 turns gives TB per cylinder near $0.05-0.1/GB; trade-offs: microsecond access, module-sized form factor.

title: AIST Minimal Fab repurposed as regional memory repair depots
idea: Japan's Minimal Fab (half-inch wafers in desk-sized tools) failed as production because its throughput was low. Repair does not need throughput: equip US regional depots with minimal-fab-style tools to rework stacks, rebond patch tiles, replace dies and re-ball modules.
why: Makes repairable designs economically real and builds US memory manufacturing jobs and capability at low capital (~$10-50M per depot).

title: Zipper teeth: capacitor meshes together at the hybrid-bond interface
idea: Like interlocking zipper teeth, each of two bonded wafers carries half of an interdigitated fin capacitor (storage-node fins on the transistor wafer, plate fins on the top wafer), both pre-coated with high-k; hybrid bonding meshes them into a capacitor of double height with no single high-AR etch.
why: Splits the 60-75:1 pillar etch (fact 1) into two ~35:1 etches; ~2x electrode area at equal etch difficulty, ~5-8 fF at relaxed aspect ratio.

title: Thermostat: per-tier refresh skipping follows the HBM stack's thermal gradient
idea: A thermostat acts on local temperature: each HBM core die reads its own sensors and tier position (top dies run 5-15 C cooler than dies near the base) and quietly executes only a fraction of the controller's REF commands, for example 1 in 2 below 70 C. Commands and timing stay JEDEC; only internal energy drops.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): 30-50% less refresh energy in cooler tiers, about 5-10% lower HBM idle power.

title: Coulomb-blockade storage dots stacked in silicon nanowire tiers
idea: Po: the charge is too lonely to leave. Store each bit as a few electrons on a <3 nm Si dot whose charging energy (>10 kT at 300 K) blocks single-electron escape, coupled by direct tunnelling to a nanowire channel in each tier, with tiers formed from Si/SiGe superlattice nanowires.
why: Refresh: the blockade adds an energy barrier for second-to-hour retention while ns direct-tunnel writes avoid the oxide wear of flash.

title: Hydra stem-cell renewal: retire rows as they age at temperature
idea: Hydra avoids ageing by continuously replacing worn cells from stem cells; profile every row's retention in the background at 125 C and progressively retire rows whose retention or variable-retention-time behaviour degrades into a 2-3% spare-row pool, updating a per-bank remap table over the decade.
why: Retention tails widen over 10 yrs at 125 C (aging, VRT); continuous renewal keeps refresh at a tail-free rate instead of guard-banding for end-of-life tails, ~2x refresh savings.

title: Pillars first, tiers grown around them
idea: Invert stack-then-etch: start with short vertical Mo bitline pillar stubs on the base, then build each tier bottom-up around them (deposit and planarize dielectric and channel), extending each pillar by area-selective deposition per tier, so no 60+ tier high-aspect-ratio hole etch is ever needed.
why: 3D process wall (fact 2): removes the HAR etch and its hardmask cost; tier count is limited by deposition cycles rather than etch AR.

title: Undiced wafer-scale DRAM fused with bonded defect-routing mesh
idea: Never dice: keep a whole 300 mm DRAM wafer, hybrid-bond a router-mesh wafer above it (Cerebras-style), and route around bad mats, so the wafer, package and module become one ~1 TB memory plane fed by edge optical links.
why: Removes dicing, packaging, TSVs and KGD test (fact 6); ~100% of good mats usable after sparing; cost per bit claimed -20-30% and ~1 pJ/bit on-wafer transport.

title: Swiss cheese: two partial-good dies packaged as one standard DDR5 die
idea: Cheese with holes still sells by the block: bin dies with dead banks or mats, then package two complementary partial dies with a tiny bridge die that steers each bank address to whichever die has it working. The package is one standard 16/24/32 Gb DDR5 device, and dies scrapped today become product.
why: Bit supply: effective wafer output +5-10% at near-zero capex, the fastest supply lever.

title: In-plane side-gated tiers: wordline silicided from the tier itself
idea: Limit: zero tungsten. Next to each tier's lateral channel, a parallel strip of the same Si tier, across a narrow ALD-dielectric-filled slit, is converted to NiSi and becomes an in-plane side-gate wordline. No metal fill goes into deep recesses.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China about 80%) and Fact 2: removes W replacement-gate fill and its void and stress problems in high-tier stacks.

title: Rambus royalty lesson: open, interchangeable core-die standard for repairable stacks
idea: Rambus's royalty model and HMC's closed spec both slowed adoption. Define an open, royalty-free mechanical and electrical standard for the DRAM core dies inside a stack, so any vendor's die can replace a failed one. US government and hyperscaler buyers then require serviceable stacks built to this standard.
why: Turns stacks into repairable assemblies with multi-vendor supply, letting small US fabs sell core dies (U.S. manufacturability) and raising uptime per scarce bit.

title: Castellated kerf vias: TSVs moved to die edges
idea: Move vertical interconnect from die interior to edge: one added mask etches via trenches in the dicing streets, and sawing through their centers leaves half-vias on each die's sidewall. After stacking, the aligned sidewall half-vias are connected vertically by plating or printed redistribution.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): frees interior TSV keep-out area for cells and avoids TSV-induced stress and yield loss.

title: Kangaroo pouch: spare-subarray chiplet carried beside the HBM base die
idea: A pouch carries a spare: co-package a small 'spare' DRAM chiplet bonded under or beside the HBM base die, and give the base die a CAM that redirects any failed core-die subarray to spare subarrays within the tRCD budget. Hosts see a standard HBM3E stack, and failures found after stacking are repaired instead of scrapped.
why: HBM yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6): claim stack yield above 90% and cost per good HBM bit -15 to -25%.

title: Retention-tail sparing at word granularity in the base die
idea: Po: the weak cells simply don't exist. After stacking, measure every 64-bit word's retention at 95 C over repeated passes, remap the worst ~0.1% (the fA tail plus variable-retention words) to a spare tier through a CAM in the logic base die, so every remaining word retains >10 s and refresh is disabled for shorter-lived data.
why: Refresh: repairs the tail (fact 3) instead of refreshing for it; one spare tier per 32 is cheap in 3D. Variable retention time is the main risk.

title: Spare tiers with post-stack tier-remapping fuses
idea: Worse: stack tiers or dies blindly so one bad layer scraps the whole stack (yield^N). Flip: build every stack with 1-2 spare tiers and a tier-map fuse ROM in the base die, test after stacking, and logically swap failed tiers out exactly as spare rows are swapped today.
why: HBM stack yield loss is 20-30% (fact 6): 0.97^12 ~69% becomes >95% with two spares at ~15% bit overhead; the same scheme makes 100+ tier monolithic stacks yieldable.

title: Creme brulee torch: laser-grown single grains form monolithic cell tiers
idea: A torch caramelizes only the top: deposit amorphous Si over the finished periphery and lower array, then melt it with an excimer laser through a micro-Czochralski grain filter (a seed hole at each cell site), growing one single-crystal grain under each future access transistor at a BEOL thermal budget. Extra cell tiers stack above, and the die is still a standard DDR5 part at ~2x density.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): near-single-crystal upper-tier transistors without wafer bonding; claim 2-4 tiers at <450 C for ~1.8x bits per die area.

title: Laser-grown location-controlled silicon grains for stacked single-crystal tiers
idea: [Box: 1T1C or 2T0C | grain-boundary-free Si FET | standard SA | monolithic sequential tiers | Si | excimer laser + DUV grain-filter holes (micro-Czochralski)] On each new tier, deposit a-Si over a small DUV-patterned grain-filter hole at every transistor site and melt it with an excimer laser, so one grain grows from each hole and a single-crystal island lands exactly where each transistor goes.
why: 3D (fact 2) without EUV: near-single-crystal, low-leakage transistors on every tier at relaxed DUV pitch, with density from tier count.

title: BeSang monolithic 3D fixed with seeded rapid-melt-growth tiers
idea: BeSang and other monolithic-3D ventures failed because low-temperature upper tiers had poor polysilicon transistors. Open seed windows to the single-crystal tier below and deposit amorphous Si over the oxide. Melt it with nanosecond laser pulses so it regrows laterally as single crystal from each seed (rapid-melt growth), while lower tiers stay under 450C.
why: Gives crystalline access transistors in every tier of 26+ tier 3D DRAM (fact 2) without a wafer bond per tier. Leakage approaches bulk Si (fact 3).

title: Fire-brigade bucket chain: CCD charge transfer to a tiny sense node
idea: Like a bucket brigade passing water hand to hand, read a vertical 16-cell string CCD-style: 4-phase 0.5 V transfer gates clock the selected cell's charge along a buried channel to a ~0.3 fF floating diffusion with a source follower and correlated double sampling, and reverse clocking writes it back.
why: Energy per access (facts 8, 10): no bitline swing at all, only low-voltage transfer gates and a tiny high-gain node; claims >10x lower read energy and supports ~0.2 fF cells.

title: In-stack voltage-window decoder replaces wordline staircase
idea: Limit: zero staircase area. Each tier is grown with in-situ graded doping so its select device has a distinct threshold. Two series select gates in the same film, one inversion-mode and one junctionless depletion-mode, open a voltage window that turns on exactly one tier. So two vertical gate electrodes address 64+ tiers with no stair contacts.
why: Fact 7 and 3D cost: staircase plus contacts can take 10-20% of a 3D die and grows with tier count; this makes tier addressing O(1) area.

title: Artillery-fuze lesson: mold-retained honeycomb braces AR-120 capacitors
idea: Artillery-fuze electronics survive 20,000 g by having no unsupported tall structure; likewise keep the oxide mold in place as a hexagonal honeycomb that braces every storage node, so tall electrodes cannot lean, bend or stick during wet cleans. Electrodes line each honeycomb cup, and the extra height (AR 120 instead of ~65) more than repays the lost outer surface.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): reaches the needed AR ~115 without pattern collapse, ~1.4x Cs or ~20% tighter pitch.

title: Termite mound chimneys: convective cooling shafts through tall stacks
idea: Termites cool their mounds with vertical chimneys. Etch dummy vertical shafts every ~200 um through the 3D array stack and fill them with a sealed two-phase working fluid (micro heat pipes) that carries heat to a top cold plate.
why: Retention roughly doubles for every ~10C cooler. Holding inner tiers ~20C cooler cuts refresh energy and bandwidth loss ~4x and allows taller stacks (Fact 3).

title: Open tier-stack standard on a shared U.S. pilot line
idea: Worse: keep every company's 3D DRAM base stack secret so each one separately relearns 100-tier deposition, slit etch and staircase. Flip: a U.S. consortium standardizes the base stack (superlattice, slits, staircase, bond interface) as a foundry PDK on a shared pilot line, and members differentiate only on the cell module inserted into it.
why: Splits the $15B+, 3-5 year learning curve (fact 4) across members and builds U.S. manufacturability from today's 1-2% share.

title: LNG cryogenic logistics: 77 K racks enable capacitor-less tiers
idea: Borrowed from LNG handling: memory sleds run immersed in liquid nitrogen, where subthreshold leakage falls by many orders of magnitude, so a bare floating node in a 3D tier holds charge for seconds to hours with no capacitor at all.
why: Removes the capacitor (facts 1-2) and nearly all refresh (fact 3); wire resistance drops ~6x; cooling overhead ~10-20% of saved power.

title: Minify temperature to 77 K, minify capacitor to 0.5 fF
idea: Run whole memory sleds immersed in liquid nitrogen. At 77 K, junction and subthreshold leakage fall by more than six orders of magnitude, so a planar 0.5 fF capacitor holds data for hours, and a 4F2 cell needs no high-AR pillar at all.
why: Capacitor wall and refresh: refresh disappears, the capacitor process collapses to planar, and density could reach about 1.5x 6F2. The cost is cryocooling at datacenter scale.

title: CVD diamond interlayers between DRAM tiers to spread heat
idea: [Box: standard cell | any access device | any sensing | wafer stack with 1-2 um polycrystalline diamond bonding layers | Si + diamond | low-temperature diamond growth + through-diamond vias] Insert thin diamond heat spreaders (k ~1000 W/mK) between stacked dies or wafers so hotspots from logic underneath no longer raise local array temperature.
why: Retention roughly halves per ~10 C; cutting array temperature 15-20 C reduces refresh 2-4x (fact 3) and lets HBM-on-logic stacks grow taller (fact 6).

title: Puff pastry: exponential lamination reaches 128 tiers in seven bonds
idea: Fold-and-roll multiplies pastry layers exponentially: build a 2-tier single-crystal cell stack, bond it face-down onto an identical stack and split off the donor to get 4 tiers, then repeat 4-on-4 and 8-on-8. 128 tiers take 7 bonding steps instead of 128 depositions, and every tier keeps a single-crystal channel.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): single-crystal lateral transistors far beyond the 26-tier breakeven with log2 process steps; claim cost per bit -40% versus 2D.

title: Mars-ISRU gas whitelist as a rare-gas-free DRAM process kit
idea: A Mars fab could only use gases made from CO2, water and nitrogen; define a binding whitelist (N2, H2, O2, CO2, H2O, NH3, NF3, HF, HBr, Cl2, SiH4) and requalify every 3D-array step against it, publishing the recipes as an open process design kit. Make whitelist compliance a condition of federal fab grants so U.S. DRAM lines cannot be stopped by a helium, neon or xenon shock.
why: Helium (Qatar ~30% offline), neon and xenon chokepoints removed and U.S. manufacturability raised; a step change in supply resilience rather than cost.

title: Audio-RAM revival: stack fab fallout dies onto ECC base die
idea: Revive 1980s 'ARAM' (partly failing DRAM sold for answering machines) and Sinclair's half-good chips: buy wafer-sort fallout and retired dies whose cells fail at up to 1%, hybrid-bond them onto a logic base die with strong LDPC and remap tables, and sell the stacks as CXL capacity.
why: Scarce supply: raises usable DRAM bits ~5-10% with zero new fab capital; base-die correction hides the 1% BER from hosts.

title: Every LCD pixel is a DRAM cell: display-fab memory sheets
idea: Scale from wafer up to Gen 8.5 display glass: an active-matrix pixel is a transistor plus a storage capacitor, so idle display fabs with 1-2 um litho can make giant oxide-TFT 1T1C sheets. Dice and laminate 32 sheets into a bulk tier for capacity-hungry, latency-tolerant work such as KV-cache spill.
why: Capital and supply (facts 4, 6): display area costs ~100x less per cm2 than DRAM wafers, adding capacity without new DRAM fabs; the honest catch is low density per layer.

title: Vertical charge-coupled shift columns with zero transistors per bit
idea: Limit: no access transistor per bit. Each 4F2 column is a stack of 3-phase clocked gate tiers forming CCD potential wells. Charge packets shift down the column at about 2 GHz to one sense node at its base, giving page access in about 10-30 ns.
why: Facts 1-3: about 20 bits per 4F2 footprint with no capacitor or transistor per bit; endurance is unlimited because the storage is charge.

title: Refresh-free device class written into standards and procurement
idea: Po: refresh is outlawed. Propose a JEDEC device class 'RF0' plus a CHIPS procurement preference: devices advertise per-region guaranteed retention, controllers carry data-expiry semantics (reads after expiry return poison), and refresh commands are optional, creating a market for long-retention 3D cells and lifetime-aware software.
why: Refresh power and bandwidth (fact 3) at system scale; policy pull for new U.S.-made cell types.

title: Capacitor first, IGZO transistor last, perovskite dielectric
idea: Re-sequence the flow: build the capacitor array first in the silicon wafer and crystallize a SrTiO3 dielectric (k~100+) at 700 C, then build low-temperature (<400 C) IGZO vertical access transistors on top by re-using the existing active/wordline/bitline masks; the only added mask is the via from capacitor top to transistor drain.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) and leakage tail (fact 3): reaches k~100 with no 1000 C anneal hitting the transistor; IGZO off-current (<1e-19 A/um) shrinks the leakage tail.

title: Memory on the cold side: thermal-break 3D DRAM beneath logic
idea: Worse: stack DRAM directly on a 700 W accelerator so it bakes at 95 C and refreshes 4x more often. Flip: hybrid-bond the DRAM tiers to the logic through a low-thermal-conductivity bonding interlayer that only signal vias cross, and cool the DRAM from its own backside cold plate while logic heat exits the opposite face.
why: Retention roughly halves per ~10 C; holding DRAM at ~55 C instead of 95 C cuts refresh ~10x (fact 3: refresh is 16-33% of idle power) while keeping on-logic data-movement savings (fact 5).

title: Potter's coil: self-rolling strained membrane turns planar array into tiers
idea: The potter builds tall vessels by coiling. Fabricate a planar gain-cell array on a pre-strained SiN/Si bilayer nanomembrane and release it with a sacrificial undercut so it self-rolls into a ~20-turn scroll. Wordlines run continuously along the spiral and contacts sit only at the outer edge.
why: One planar litho pass gives ~20 effective tiers with no staircase and no per-tier masks (Facts 2, 4).

title: Toshiba chain-FeRAM revived as vertical chains of antiferroelectric cells
idea: Toshiba's chain-FeRAM (each cell a transistor in parallel with a ferroelectric capacitor, cells in series like NAND) died with PZT's hydrogen damage and a 2D footprint. Build it vertically: a pillar of gate-all-around tiers, each shunting a thin antiferroelectric ZrO2 capacitor ring, with one contact per chain. To read a tier, its shunt turns off while the others stay on.
why: One bitline contact per 16-32 tiers removes the 3D staircase/contact blocker (fact 2). AFE ZrO2 switches fast with high endurance and contains no lead.

title: Rutile TiO2 on MnO2 template replaces Hf/Zr and Ru
idea: Inverts 'high-k capacitors need Hf/Zr oxides on Ru electrodes.' Seed rutile-phase Al-doped TiO2 (k~90-120) on a thin rutile-structured beta-MnO2 template over TiN, so abundant Mn does the templating job RuO2 does today.
why: Fact 1 and scarce resources: reaches the k~70 target, so pillar AR can drop from ~70:1 to ~40:1 with no Hf, Zr or Ru.

title: Complementary gain cell: p-WSe2 write tier over n-IGZO read tier
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: make the write transistor p-type (WSe2 or SnO) in one tier and the read transistor n-type IGZO in the tier below, stacked in one footprint. The p-type device passes a full 1 with its wordline at 0 V instead of a ~3 V boost, and its leakage polarity opposes the read device's.
why: Fact 10: removes the wordline boost (~1 V swing, ~9x less wordline CV2) and two-tier stacking halves the planar 2T0C footprint.

title: Catalyst-grown vertical nanowire transistors replace etched 4F² pillars
idea: Substitute etched Si pillars for vertical 4F² access transistors with bottom-up nanowires: Sn or Al catalyst dots placed by block-copolymer templating grow single-crystal Si nanowires (SiH4, Au-free) from bitline seeds, with in-situ B2H6/PH3 switching n+/p/n+ along the growth axis to form source/channel/drain without implants.
why: 4F² vertical-channel cell without high-AR Si etch or fluorinated gases; abrupt in-situ junctions shrink the leakage tail (fact 3); non-gold catalysts avoid deep-level traps.

title: Magnify cell to 16F2 at F=40nm, magnify tiers to 120
idea: Deliberately enlarge the cell to 16F2 at a 40 nm half-pitch printable with dry ArF (no immersion, no EUV), then make it up in height by stacking 120 deposition-defined lateral-cell tiers, where each tier needs no new critical mask because only the deposition loop repeats. 16F2 at 40 nm is about 25,600 nm2 per tier, so 120 tiers gives roughly 4x the bit density of 6F2 at 12 nm.
why: Capital and litho wall: removes all 5-7 EUV layers and swaps them for repeated depositions, so depreciation per bit could drop by 2-3x while density still rises about 4x.

title: Eliminate the 3D staircase: contact tiers at the etched die sidewall
idea: Remove the NAND-style staircase entirely; terminate every tier at a deep-etched trench wall at the mat edge where all tiers are exposed edge-on, then a laser-written or tilted-deposition redistribution layer fans each tier out to the top surface.
why: No manufacturable 3D DRAM: the staircase costs area and N trim/etch cycles; edge contacting makes tier count nearly free in area, helping reach the 26+ tier break-even.

title: Hyperscaler exabyte buyer: undiced DRAM wafers as rack memory slabs
idea: For the buyer who orders memory by the petabyte, skip dicing, per-die test and packaging: add a redistribution layer to a whole 300 mm DRAM wafer, route it to edge connectors, map bad mats in an on-wafer controller strip, and mount the bare wafer on a liquid cold plate in a CXL memory sled. A wafer of 16 Gb dies is ~1.5 TB in one field-replaceable unit.
why: Cost per bit: packaging, test and module costs (~15-25%) removed, and mat-level map-out replaces discarding whole dies (~5-10% more good bits).

title: Stack-sidewall lithography replaces TSVs in memory stacks
idea: Limit: zero TSVs. Stack dies flush, polish the stack edge, and pattern a redistribution layer directly on the stack sidewall with laser direct imaging. Each die's edge pads join vertical sidewall buses.
why: Fact 6: removes the TSV keep-out and yield tax (about 3x area per bit and 20-30% yield loss for HBM) for stacks of 12-24 dies.

title: CCD fused into 3D NAND-style string: vertical shift-register DRAM
idea: Combine a charge-coupled device with a 3D NAND gate stack: 200 tier gate planes wrap one vertical oxide-semiconductor channel, and clocking the gates shifts charge packets held in surface wells toward a floating-diffusion sense node at the top. Each gate is both 'capacitor' and transfer switch, so there is no per-cell capacitor, contact or access transistor.
why: No 3D cell (fact 2) and charge wall (fact 1): ~0.1 fF wells suffice because the floating diffusion has gain; one hole etch stores 200 bits. Serial latency ~100-200 ns, hidden by striping each cache line across 512 strings.

title: Inductive coupling coils replace HBM signal TSVs
idea: Swap the wire for a field: core dies talk vertically through on-chip coil pairs drawn in existing top metal (zero masks), and power rides highly doped silicon vias made with the one added implant mask, so the HBM stack needs no metal TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no TSV keep-out, no Cu-TSV stress or yield loss; coil links reach ~1 pJ/bit at tens of um vertical spacing.

title: Twenty-nanosecond excimer pulses crystallize each tier without cooking those below
idea: Shift the thermal timescale from hour-long furnace anneals to 20-ns XeCl excimer pulses, a 1990s LTPS display tool: deposit amorphous Si for each new tier and melt-recrystallize it in nanoseconds so heat never reaches the tiers below. Stack 16-32 poly-Si 1T1C tiers this way.
why: Thermal budget blocks sequential 3D (fact 2): monolithic tiers become possible with display-era tools.

title: Roof-shingle HBM: offset die stacks with 3D-printed edge traces
idea: Stack legacy DDR4/LPDDR dies offset like roof shingles so each die's edge pad row is exposed, then aerosol-jet 3D-print 20 um-pitch copper traces down the staircase to a logic base die, giving a wide bus without TSVs.
why: Removes TSV area and yield tax (fact 6) with installed OSAT tools; ~1-2k traces per edge gives HBM2-class bandwidth from mature dies.

title: Gaines stochastic bitstreams multiplied by ANDing vertical tier strings
idea: Revive Gaines' 1960s stochastic computing: weights and activations are stored as random bitstreams laid along vertical strings, so multiplying two values is a single AND of two strings sensed together in the array, and a 1% cell BER shifts a value by only ~1%.
why: Fact 5: avoids moving operands off-die for low-precision ops (>=5x less data-movement energy) on cheap, error-prone tiers.

title: Goto-pair interband tunneling diodes atop a vertical access transistor
idea: TRIZ #40 Composite materials: grow two series Si/SiGe resonant interband tunneling diodes directly on top of a 4F2 vertical access transistor. Their negative-differential-resistance curves make the midpoint node bistable, a static latch inside the vertical stack held by a tiny supply current.
why: Fact 3: refresh-free, capacitor-free 4F2 cell with statically held state; access energy ~1/3 of 1T1C because there is no restore cycle.

title: Capacitor-first substrate: MacEtch forest with the wafer as plate
idea: Under 400 C, metal-assisted chemical etching (Au mesh in HF/H2O2 at room temperature) drills 20 nm holes at AR about 150 into a doped Si wafer. After an ALD MIM liner at 300 C, the oxide transistor tier is built on top, and the bulk wafer itself is the common cell plate.
why: Fact 1: breaks the 60-75:1 etch limit with a wet bench instead of a $10M+ etcher; Cs 8-10 fF.

title: CDO tranching: retention-binned die pools before stacking
idea: Treat dies like loan pools: measure each array die's retention tail and speed at wafer sort, sort into tranches and build stacks only from matching tranches (senior tranche to HBM with relaxed refresh, junior to consumer DRAM), instead of stacking randomly and binning the stack by its worst die.
why: HBM yield (fact 6) and refresh (fact 3): stacks stop inheriting the worst die; claims 10-15% more sellable stacks and a premium tier with 2x refresh interval.

title: Magnify redundancy to 30% spare tiers with boot-time self-repair
idea: Design 3D DRAM with about 30% spare tiers and rows, plus a built-in self-test that remaps failing rows at every power-on, so a stack can tolerate a defect density about 10x higher than 2D DRAM.
why: Unlocks a 3D manufacturing cell that is not yet manufacturable: cheaper, less perfect deposition could ship sooner at about 70% usable density.

title: TSV keep-out rings fused with segmented deep-trench storage capacitors
idea: Combine the HBM TSV and the cell capacitor: etch an annular deep trench (AR ~50) in the dead keep-out zone around each TSV, split it into 16-32 sectors with vertical dielectric fins, and use each sector as a storage capacitor read through vertical transistors on the ring rim. One structure is the TSV stress shield, a decoupling cap and bit storage.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): turns the ~10-15% of die lost to TSV fields and keep-out zones into bits; claimed +5-8% bits per HBM core die plus free decap.

title: Let bits decay and recover them with cross-tier erasure codes
idea: Po: memory that is allowed to rot. Disable refresh and stripe each 64 B line across 12 tiers with an 8+4 Reed-Solomon erasure code plus weak-cell location maps from test, so the retention tail is corrected at read while the median cell holds data for minutes, longer than most working sets live.
why: Refresh zero by converting the leakage tail into a coding problem; 50% parity overhead is offset by cheap tiers and removed refresh periphery.

title: 64-cell vertical bitlines let 1.5 fF capacitors suffice
idea: Limit: Cs may not exceed 1.5 fF. Make every bitline vertical and only as long as the tier count (64 cells, about 2 um), so bitline capacitance falls to about 3 fF versus about 50-80 fF planar. The transfer ratio Cs/(Cs+Cb) jumps about 5x, and a lateral capacitor that fits inside a tier gives enough signal.
why: Facts 1 and 2: breaks the 4.5-5.4 fF requirement that blocks 3D lateral capacitors and keeps about 150 mV of read signal.

title: Aluminum layer exchange crystallizes each tier's silicon below 450 C
idea: For each stacked tier, sputter Al, let a thin oxide membrane form, sputter a-Si on top and anneal at ~425 C so Si diffuses through the Al and crystallizes beneath it as large-grain (>10 um) (111)-textured poly-Si; etch away the displaced Al, counter-dope the Al background and build lateral transistors in the grains.
why: Near-crystalline lateral channels for every 3D tier (fact 2) inside BEOL thermal budget over finished periphery, using only sputter, furnace and wet etch.

title: One transistor gates a string of resonance-staggered capacitors
idea: Po: one transistor, many capacitors. Above each vertical access transistor stack 4-8 capacitors, each behind a double-barrier resonant-tunnelling selector with a different resonance voltage set by well width, so the bitline bias chooses which single capacitor conducts: 1T-8C per footprint.
why: Density (fact 4): ~4-8x bits per transistor footprint without extra litho; risk is resonance selectivity and peak-to-valley ratio at room temperature.

title: Cymer-laser interference lithography plus Multibeam e-beam cuts for arrays
idea: Combine maskless two-beam 193 nm interference lithography (ArF lasers built in San Diego) for the perfectly periodic wordline, bitline and pillar gratings with US multi-column e-beam direct-write (Multibeam, Santa Clara) for the sparse cuts, contacts and periphery, plus one spacer doubling to reach ~20 nm half-pitch.
why: Fact 4: removes 5-7 EUV layers and the photomask set; interference tool estimated <$10M; e-beam writes only the ~5% irregular features, so throughput stays workable for an all-US flow.

title: Wavelength-coded absorber tiers enable stack-first, anneal-later 3D DRAM
idea: TRIZ #32 Color changes: give each tier an absorber with a distinct optical resonance (SiGe of graded Ge %, tuned-thickness TiN, plasmonic nanodisks), deposit the whole stack cold, then crystallize or activate each tier's channel with a laser tuned to that tier. Neighboring tiers are transparent at that wavelength and stay cool.
why: Fact 2: removes the thermal-budget conflict of monolithic tiers; one-pass deposition cuts cycle time and capital per tier ~30-50%.

title: Two-bit cells in long lateral 3D capacitors via time-to-threshold sensing
idea: [Box: four-level charge | IGZO lateral FET | time-domain SA (bitline crossing timed by per-tier counter) | monolithic 3D | Si | ALD] Lateral capacitors in 3D DRAM can be made long (Cs ~15-20 fF) for little extra cost; spend that charge on four levels and read them by timing when the bitline crosses a single reference.
why: 3D break-even (fact 2): 2 bits per cell cuts tiers needed to beat planar from ~26 to ~13.

title: Mirror-bond two VCT array wafers at their common blanket plate
idea: [Box: MIM charge | 4F2 VCT | charge-share SA | face-to-face bond at the capacitor plate | Si | blanket TiN-to-TiN bond needing no fine alignment] Finish two VCT arrays with an unpatterned top plate and bond them plate-to-plate; since the shared plate is blanket, overlay can be off by microns, and the upper array's bitlines reach periphery through coarse vias at the array edge.
why: Doubles bits per footprint at the same DUV pitch with one alignment-tolerant bond, beating the ~10-20% a node shrink buys (fact 4).

title: 1T-TaS2 charge-density-wave hidden-state switching in vdW tiers
idea: Charge density waves: picosecond electrical pulses drive 1T-TaS2 flakes into a metastable hidden CDW state whose resistance differs by orders of magnitude, and a longer pulse restores the ground state. Transferable van der Waals flakes can be stacked as many thin non-volatile tiers.
why: Gives ps-scale switching with non-volatile tiers of atomic thickness (facts 2 and 10); claim fJ writes. Room-temperature stability of the hidden state is speculative.
